data.title: How Mud Becomes a Semiconductor Factory

sentences.text: If you dig a pit and let muddy water settle, you have a sandy floor.
But sand is silicon locked to oxygen, so no current passes through it.
It is full of clay and iron, yet a chip allows only one foreign atom per billion.
So you pour the sand into a furnace with carbon.
Then you heat it up to about 2,000 °C, and the oxygen burns off as gas.
But now that gas is loose, so you pipe it into a second tank where pure silicon forms.
So you melt the pure silicon and pull one single crystal out of it.
This is a Czochralski crystal puller.
Slice the crystal into thin discs, and each disc is a wafer.
Machines print layer after layer of tiny switches onto each wafer with light.
One modern chip can hold over 20 billion of those switches.
But a single speck of dust landing on a wafer can kill the chip.
In an open hall, wind and rain blow in mud and ruin a whole batch.
So you build a roof over the hall and push filtered air down, making a cleanroom.
And beach sand is not chip sand, whatever everyone knows.
The purest quartz comes from Spruce Pine, North Carolina, which supplies an estimated 70 to 90 percent of the world's high-purity quartz.
Add ceiling lights and stepping stones, and the pit runs clear.
Congratulations, you have built a semiconductor factory.
